summary: Pheromones are secreted or excreted chemicals that trigger social responses in members of the same species, used from bacteria to vertebrates and especially well documented in insects. The note classifies them by function (aggregation, alarm, epideictic, territorial, trail, sex) and by type (releaser, primer, signal), and covers their receptors, evolution and applications such as pest traps. It ends with the unresolved debate over human pheromones, where no substance has been shown in a peer reviewed study to directly influence human behavior.
one_line: Overview of pheromones: chemical signals within a species, their functional and type classifications, receptors, evolution, applications, and the controversy over human pheromones.
key_facts: The word 'pheromone' was coined by Peter Karlson and Martin Lüscher in 1959, from Greek phérō ('I carry') and hórmōn ('stimulating').
Adolf Butenandt characterized bombykol, the first such chemical, a pheromone released by the female silkworm to attract mates.
Aggregation pheromones are used to manage pests such as the boll weevil (Anthonomus grandis) and are non-toxic and effective at very low concentrations.
Alarmed pronghorn (Antilocapra americana) release an alarm compound, 2-pyrrolidinone, with an odor 'reminiscent of buttered popcorn', detectable 20 to 30 meters downwind.
Ants mark trails with volatile hydrocarbon pheromones that evaporate quickly and need continuous renewal; Pharaoh ants (Monomorium pharaonis) mark dead-end trails with a repellent pheromone.
Some lepidopterans (moths and butterflies) can detect a potential mate from as far away as 10 km (6.2 mi).
Primer pheromones change developmental events rather than behavior; they were first described in Schistocerca gregaria by Maud Norris in 1954.
Humans have six trace amine-associated receptors (TAAR1, TAAR2, TAAR5, TAAR6, TAAR8, TAAR9); all except TAAR1 are expressed in the olfactory epithelium.

The vomeronasal organ (Jacobson's organ) detects pheromones in reptiles, amphibia and non-primate mammals; it is absent in birds, adult catarrhine monkeys and apes, and its role in humans is disputed.
Mice use scent to distinguish close relatives and avoid inbreeding, as do the bumblebees Bombus bifarius and Bombus frigidus.
The McClintock effect, named after Martha McClintock of the University of Chicago, proposed menstrual synchronization via odor cues, but recent reviews question its validity.
Possible human pheromones include axillary steroids (androstadienol, androstadienone, androstenol, androstenone, androsterone) and vaginal aliphatic acids called 'copulins'.
Genes encoding VNO receptors are nonfunctional pseudogenes in humans, and the VNO appears to lack connections to the central nervous system.
Claus Wedekind and colleagues found that men and women prefer the axillary odors of people whose MHC differs from their own.

entities.name: Peter Karlson
entities.role: coined the term 'pheromone' in 1959 with Martin Lüscher

entities.name: Adolf Butenandt
entities.role: German biochemist who characterized bombykol, the first pheromone

entities.name: Karl von Frisch
entities.role: ethologist who studied early pheromones, calling them 'alarm substances'

entities.name: Jean-Henri Fabre
entities.role: early researcher who observed epideictic pheromones in egg-laying females

entities.name: Maud Norris
entities.role: first described primer pheromones in Schistocerca gregaria in 1954

entities.name: Martha McClintock
entities.role: University of Chicago investigator behind the McClintock effect on menstrual synchronization

entities.name: Claus Wedekind
entities.role: found people prefer axillary odors of those with different MHC

entities.name: Milinski
entities.role: researcher who found chosen artificial odors are shaped partly by MHC combination

entities.name: Kirk-Smith
entities.role: conducted a 1978 study of androstenol-treated masks and ratings of pictures

entities.name: Bombykol
entities.role: well-characterized pheromone released by female silkworms

entities.name: Vomeronasal organ
entities.role: accessory olfactory organ that detects pheromones in many animals

entities.name: Trace amine-associated receptors
entities.role: olfactory epithelium receptors that may detect pheromones

entities.name: Eciton burchellii
entities.role: army ant that uses pheromones to maintain foraging paths

entities.name: Bombus hyperboreus
entities.role: bumblebee whose drones patrol pheromone scent marks to find queens
